title: Spain’s RTVE Joins Netflix, Universal on Félix Viscarret’s ETA Drama ‘Blanco’
description: Spanish public broadcaster RTVE has boarded “Blanco,” a high-profile feature directed by Félix Viscarret (“Patria,” “Under the Stars”) about the 199
body:
Spanish public broadcaster RTVE has boarded “Blanco,” a high-profile feature directed by Félix Viscarret (“Patria,” “Under the Stars”) about the 1997 kidnapping and murder of Basque politician Miguel Ángel Blanco by terrorist organization ETA.

	RTVE joins Netflix and Universal Pictures International Spain on the project, with Universal set to handle its theatrical distribution. The film is produced by Kiko Martínez’s Nadie es Perfecto (“The Bar,” “Perfect Strangers”) and Eduardo Carneros-led Euskadi Movie.
	

	The combination of major industry partners, a subject of enduring significance in Spain and an anniversary release date gives “Blanco” the potential of becoming a major theatrical event.


	Universal will open the film in Spanish cinemas on July 9, 2027, with the release timed around the 30th anniversary of the kidnapping and murder. Production is scheduled to begin on Oct. 5, 2026, with the cast set to be announced shortly.

	Budgeted at €8 million ($9.2 million), “Blanco” will reconstruct the 48 hours that held Spain in suspense after ETA abducted Blanco, a 29-year-old councillor for the conservative Partido Popular in the Basque town of Ermua, in July 1997.

	ETA demanded that the Spanish government transferred the organization’s prisoners to jails in the Basque Country, threatening to kill Blanco unless its conditions were met within two days. He was shot after the deadline expired and died on July 13.

	The crime prompted an extraordinary wave of demonstrations across Spain and became a turning point in the country’s public response to ETA terrorism.
	

	Drawing on extensive journalistic research and first-hand accounts, “Blanco” will follow the reporters who covered the kidnapping, the efforts to save Blanco and the aftermath of his murder. The project has the support of his family, represented by his sister María del Mar Blanco.

	“Through the eyes of these journalists, we will meet people, many of them anonymous, who tried to stop the horror or prevent the suffering that followed from provoking still more violence,” Viscarret said.

	“Although they may have believed at the time that they had failed, their acts of courage, compassion and responsibility helped transform the sensibility of a society, demonstrating that even in the darkest moments, human beings are capable of bringing out the best in themselves.”

	Martínez said the film’s strength lies in placing viewers alongside those charged with reporting the crisis as it unfolded.

	“Through their perspective, we will witness an event that shook the whole of Spanish society and changed the course of our recent history,” he said.

	RTVE frames “Blanco” as part of its push into ambitious Spanish films tackling major events from the country’s recent history.

schema.headline: Spain’s RTVE Joins Netflix, Universal on Félix Viscarret’s ETA Drama ‘Blanco’

title: CBS Bets Tony Dokoupil’s ‘Big Question’ Segment Makes Sizable Difference in Evening-News Battle
description:
Tony Dokoupil’s job hinges on breaking news. He has recently been taking precious seconds to try and knit some of it together.

	On a recent Friday
body:
Tony Dokoupil’s job hinges on breaking news. He has recently been taking precious seconds to try and knit some of it together.

	On a recent Friday night, the “CBS Evening News” anchor stopped the rat-a-tat-tat delivery of headlines for which his program and similar ones are known, just to reflect. He delivered a short monologue focused on the ramped-up construction of data centers across the U.S. Dokoupil simply wanted an answer to the following: “In an election year where Americans are mostly divided on the issues, why are so many united around opposition” to the new facilities?
	

	To answer the query, Dokoupil relied on video, charts and an oral essay expressed in his own writing. Americans, Dokoupil said, “oppose them because they are as big as airports, draw more power than a small city, use as much water as the same and support a technology, AI, whose own founders say could be an existential risk to life here on earth.”


	Since July 1, “CBS Evening News” has rolled out four segments of this type — known as “The Big Question” — and producers hope they will serve to grab viewers with frank discussions tied to the news of the day.

	There are many questions Americans ask in their daily conversations “that for whatever reason don’t get baldly and directly asked in the press,” says Dokoupil, 45, during a recent interview. “I’m talking about the origin of COVID, the Wuhan question. Is Joe Biden mentally capable of another term? How is it legal for Donald Trump to enrich himself and his family while in office? These are questions people are talking about, but don’t feel like they can be asked. There is a cost to asking them. We decided we’re going to ask them and we going to do our best to give people an answer.” In some cases, the monologue will do the trick; in others, Dokoupil may enlist a topic expert to help figure things out.
	

	“Big Question” segments have been devoted to asking whether the Trump administration can really win a battle for the Strait of Hormuz; why Democrats stood by Graham Plantner, the Maine candidate for U.S. Senator even as troubling elements of his background were revealed; and whether President Trump’s gains from cryptocurrency ventures are legal and ethical. Such an element is not usual for evening news, and that is one reason why it’s of interest, says Kim Harvey, the show’s executive producer: “We get a chance to distinguish ourselves from our competitors and also serve our audience in a better way.”

	Evening news viewers expect the anchors to deliver headlines, but not necessarily to use them as jumping-off points for analysis. Walter Cronkie told viewers “That’s the way it is” every evening but did not push the audience to consider why things were that way. NBC News’ Lester Holt attempted to introduce some analysis to “NBC Nightly News” in the back half of his tenure, offering at times a bit of commentary on particularly troubling events, such as the rise of deaths from coronavirus or the collapse of the Francis Scott Key Bridge near Baltimore. The idea, Holt told Variety last year, was to acknowledge tragedy or uncommon events.

	One industry consultant believes news shows ought to embrace such stuff — and with more speed. The evening-news shows “certainly serve an audience, but it is an audience that’s aging, and we have this large audience of younger people who have been underserved in their minds by traditional media platforms,” says Jaime Spencer, chief operating officer of Magid, which advises TV stations and media companies. “They are relying very heavily on creators, social media, and those types of providers who are more charged with opinion.” A “Big Question” segment at ‘CBS Evening News” will offer viewers something beyond the headlines they’ve likely already seen online during their day.

	There’s even hope within CBS News that such segments can help the division reach new crowds. Dokoupil’s “Evening News” also offers “The Good Stuff,” an end-of-show segment meant to provide a moment of uplift from something going on during what the anchor always calls “another day in America.” The short pieces give older, traditional TV viewers something different to watch, and can also fit in well in digital venues, where shorter form content is the order of the day.
	

	Whether the viewer is watching linear TV or digital video, says Dokoupil, the new “Question” format “feels authentic and it feels like a person is just talking to you about the day’s events.”

	Dokoupil started his tenure at “CBS Evening News” under intense scrutiny. He was placed in the broadcast by Bari Weiss, an opinion journalist and founder of The Free Press who had recently been installed as the editor in chief of CBS News despite lacking substantial experience managing a TV newsroom. Weiss wants CBS News to be provocative and more relevant to viewers who spend more of their time on digital outlets, where individual influencers and independent journalists hold increasing sway. Weiss is known for holding pro-Israel and anti-woke stances and her reign started as Paramount CEO David Ellison made a concerted effort to appeal to the Trump administration, which has a say over whether his company can acquire Warner Bros. Discovery — the deal is now heading to a trial -– and has worked tirelessly to undermine the credibility of mainstream media outlets, including CBS News.  As a result, much of the attention paid to Dokoupil has also serves to determine how much influence Weiss has over the program and the stories it presents.

	Any new anchor would find such a scenario challenging. Dokoupil was rushed into the anchor slot quickly after the exits of predecessors John Dickerson and Maurice DuBois, who held the job before he did. The duo presided overan unorthodox two-anchor program that ceded viewers, and, eventually, ratings. Dokoupil had to work out kinks on air, in real time, and the program’s overall audience still rests below 4 million, a demarcation point for CBS News management in the past. Now the anchor and Harvey believe they’re finding new rhythm, and a routine that allows them to start adding new pieces to the show.

	“We wanted to really stabilize the broadcast and dig out of the hole we were in,” Dokoupil says.

	“CBS Evening News” has been mired in third place for decades, well behind ABC News’ top-rated “World News Tonight” with David Muir, and NBC News’ “NBC Nightly News,” anchored by Tom Llamas, who took over the show from Holt in 2025. Part of the reason for its status: CBS. Over the past decade, network executives have overhauled the program time and again, asking viewers to make connections with anchors including Scott Pelley, Norah O’Donnell and Jeff Glor, only to revise plans every few years. The show generated around $110 million in advertising in 2025, according to data from Guideline, a tracker of ad spendings. Among CBS News programs, only “CBS Mornings” brought in more.
	

	The show’s status is unlikely to change in the near term. Indeed, season to date as of July 19, “CBS Evening News” viewership among people between 25 and 54 — the demographic most coveted by advertisers in news programming — is off 13% from the year-earlier period, according to data from Nielsen. At the same time, NBC’s Llamas has made some inroads against Muir in the demo, according to Nielsen, meaning there is still some audience that is open to changing their evening habit. Executives have been encouraged in recent weeks: “CBS Evening News” in July made slight gains in overall viewership and well as its audience between 25 and 54.

	So much of evening news is devoted to an anchor making a few comments before throwing to a “package” of recorded elements from a reporter stationed outside the studio, says one person familiar with CBS News operations, and CBS hopes “to find moments to differentiate” the show from its rivals with segments that feature a different sort of voice.

	Dokoupil has tried to provide one. Many of his remarks, in which he has a strong hand in writing, contain phrases that are clever or arch. “Good evening,” he said one day while opening the program. “In the middle of war, on the eve of peace talks and as a U.S. spacecraft hurtles toward earth, First Lady Melania Trump stepped up to a bank of cameras inside the White House today to address Jeffrey Epstein — a topic that may surprise you, because it certainly surprised us.”

	When covering a push-and-pull between the Pentagon and the A.I. company Anthropic, Dokoupil told viewers that “normally a Pentagon contract story is something we’d skip, but this one could change the future of warfare, and, even in a week like this, could be the most important story we cover.” In April, he acknowledged the helter-skelter nature of President Trump’s stance toward fighting Iran. “If you are struggling to follow what’s happening, you are not alone,” he said, adding: “Here we are, about 48 hours from the deadline and seemingly as close to renewed fighting as we are to peace.”

	He hopes the storytelling on the show will help draw attention to the work of the many reporters CBS News has out in the field.

	One of Dokoupil’s first jobs was working at Newsweek on the weekly magazine’s “Periscope” section, known for offering short but stylized takes on the news, including a popular “Conventional Wisdom” feature that uses “up” and “down” arrows to show the standing of major newsmakers and closely followed topics. “I constantly return to my experience” there, Dokoupil says, noting he believes there “should be a certain bite and snap to the writing” on CBS’ evening-news program.
	

	He also hopes the “Big Question” will help forge a tighter bond with viewers in an era when a cacophony of outlets has undermined the credibility of many news sources. “You’re asking something that you know the viewers are thinking,” he explains. “You are saying to them, ‘We are looking at the same reality. I see what you’re seeing, and here’s what we know about it.’ “

	Dokoupil is likely to keep asking a “Big Question” on selected newscasts. And he will be called to answer an even bigger one: Can the anchor peel off any of the audience watching competitors like Llamas and Muir, or some of the people who favor upstart news formats?

	Evening news programs need to “take some shots,” says Spencer, the consultant. “And it’s going to take more than just exiting traditional execution to break out.”

schema.headline: CBS Bets Tony Dokoupil’s ‘Big Question’ Segment Makes Sizable Difference in Evening-News Battle

title: ‘Movies Aren’t Dead After All’: Sony Pictures Boss Tom Rothman on Historic ‘Spider-Man’ Box Office and Losing Tarantino’s Cliff Booth Sequel to Netflix
description:
“So I guess movies aren’t dead after all?”

	That’s the understated reaction from Tom Rothman, chairman of Sony Pictures, after “Spider-Man: Brand N
body:
“So I guess movies aren’t dead after all?”

	That’s the understated reaction from Tom Rothman, chairman of Sony Pictures, after “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” obliterated box office expectations. The comic book adventure, starring Tom Holland as Marvel’s web-slinging hero, ignited to $360 million domestically and a mind-blowing $932 million globally, the biggest domestic and second-largest global debut in history. And the latest Spidey entry, with help from Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” powered the largest collective weekend of all time. In other words, movies are back in the center of culture. Hallelujah!
	

	“What happened is miraculous,” says Rothman, who plans to toast the film’s thunderous start with chocolate ice cream. “‘Spider-Man’ is uniting people across cultures and ages. People can piss on theatrical all they want, but that’s one thing that only movies — and movie theaters — can do.”


	Sure, there’s been plenty of doom and gloom about the health of the theatrical business in the wake of two destructive forces: COVID and the 2023 labor strikes. But this summer is poised to be the best since the pandemic, and all kinds of hits — from “The Devil Wears Prada 2” and “Toy Story 5” to “Obsession” and “Backrooms” — have restored Hollywood’s confidence that people actually, really, truly love the big screen.

	Before rewarding himself with a frozen treat, Rothman spoke to Variety about Holland’s future as Spider-Man, Sony’s ambitions for other Marvel characters and the “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” sequel that got away.
	
	
		Tom Holland says there’s a succession plan in place for Peter Parker. But you’re not really going to let him go after a debut like this, right?	

	I love these questions. It’s like when a coach wins the Super Bowl and he goes to the press conference and they say to him, “Are you going to win it next year?” The honest truth is we don’t know at this point. This has been the focus of our studio for almost two years. I can tell you this: I certainly, certainly hope. I heard Tom say at some point that he wanted to continue, and we would love it if he did.
	
		OK, so nothing’s in place, but there is a world in which there will be another “Spider-Man” sequel with Tom Holland?	

	Yes.
	
		There’s clearly no such thing as “Spider-Man” fatigue, but what’s going on with other comic book movies? It seems like there’s no middle ground: They’re either massive successes or major bombs.	

	Superhero movies have to feel fresh. The glut of all those movies has made it even more important that they separate themselves in terms of quality. If you’re just taking the obligatory steps, the audience is less excited. You have to work against predictability. How do you make movies not feel repetitive? “Brand New Day” is emotionally led, so it feels different.
	
		I was curious about the status of Sony’s Marvel characters because —	

	You and everybody else.
	
		The “Venom” trilogy was huge, but other spinoffs like “Kraven the Hunter” and “Madame Web” were misfires. Why didn’t those work?	

	Ultimately, the audience wasn’t satisfied enough with them. Whether that’s a fair assessment of those movies, who knows. That’s howling into the wind. The audience is the boss, and they didn’t respond. It’s as simple as that.
	
		Are there plans to keep developing Sony’s universe of Marvel characters?	

	Right now, we don’t know. We never looked at it as the “Sony-Marvel Universe.” We looked at if there were worthwhile movies to make with other characters. At the moment, there are none in active development.
	
		Does this summer give you confidence about your big theatrical bet on the four-part “Beatles” movies?	

	Yes. The box office is roaring, and it makes me feel strongly that audiences want diverse, new programming. COVID was bad for the movie business, but the strikes were worse. Now there’s product, and people are remembering what fun it is. But things have to feel special. Everybody wants to make everything into an event, but to make it an event, it has to feel special. And everything about the Beatles is special. It’s a big bet, but if you’re just doing the same old, same old, audiences will stay home. Intentionality makes the audience feel that it’s not just another Friday night.
	
	
		Why is Netflix releasing “Cliff Booth,” the sequel to Sony’s “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood”?	

	Because David Fincher is exclusive to Netflix. We were going to make the movie when Quentin [Tarantino] was directing it, but he decided that he didn’t want to do it and changed course. The only other person that he was comfortable directing his script was David Fincher, and David Fincher was exclusive to Netflix, so we were not going to stand in anybody’s way.
	
		Are you disappointed that Sony doesn’t have the sequel?	

	Yes.
	
		Sony is reviving the Cinerama Dome, which has been shuttered since 2020. What does the reopening of the beloved venue mean for Hollywood?	

	It’s great, and we’re really proud. We are fully committed to theatrical, and this is the Eiffel Tower of that business. It’s sitting there in a derelict state. It was not a good message in the world and a loss of opportunity.
	
		How does the company plan to preserve the experience of watching a movie in the Dome?	

	Plans are immaculate. The idea is to restore it to its full former glory, although with every state-of-the-art update possible … projection, sound. There will be no food service. It’s going to be gorgeous.

schema.headline: ‘Movies Aren’t Dead After All’: Sony Pictures Boss Tom Rothman on Historic ‘Spider-Man’ Box Office and Losing Tarantino’s Cliff Booth Sequel to Netflix

title: ‘V/H/S/MIXTAPE’ Set at Shudder; Ninth Chapter of Horror Anthology Features RZA, Ernest Dickerson, Flying Lotus and More (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
The next “V/H/S” movie is set to bring a new beat to the series.

	Shudder has announced that the ninth installment of the horror anthology franchis
body:
The next “V/H/S” movie is set to bring a new beat to the series.

	Shudder has announced that the ninth installment of the horror anthology franchise “V/H/S/MIXTAPE” is set to debut on the streamer on Oct. 9. 

	The film includes segments from Ernest Dickerson (“Tales from the Crypt: Demon Knight”), RZA (“The Man with the Iron Fists”), David Moreau (“Mads”) and Renee Zhan (“O Black Hole!”), whose segment includes original creations from Jim Henson’s Creature Shop.
	

	Musician and director Flying Lotus (“Ash”) contributes music video interludes to the film, and debut filmmaker Tobias Forge contributes a music video. Heavy metal icons GWAR also make a featured appearance.


	The movie “cranks the signature found-footage horror up to eleven with an electrifying new anthology where music and sound become the source of terror. United by a theme that explores the power of music, rhythm, and audio to haunt, possess, and destroy, the film blends cosmic horror, psychological suspense, outrageous splatter, and groundbreaking practical effects into one unforgettable mixtape of nightmares,” per a press release.

	Producers of “V/H/S/MIXTAPE” include Josh Goldbloom, Steven Schneider, Roy Lee, Michael Schreiber and Brad Miska, as well as executive producers Ben Ross and Rami Yassin.

	Last year’s “V/H/S/Halloween” was a hit for Shudder and AMC+, as it was the most-watched exclusive film premiere of 2025 on the platforms. It also drove Shudder’s biggest acquisition weekend of the year.

	The series began with 2012’s “V/H/S,” which included segments from Ti West, Radio Silence, Joe Swanberg and more.
	

	Watch the trailer for the previous installment, “V/H/S/Halloween,” below.

schema.headline: ‘V/H/S/MIXTAPE’ Set at Shudder; Ninth Chapter of Horror Anthology Features RZA, Ernest Dickerson, Flying Lotus and More (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Talking Tom & Friends: World’ Kids’ Mobile Game Launches The Smurfs Crossover (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
“Talking Tom & Friends: World” has launched an in-game crossover with the iconic world of The Smurfs.

	In a partnership between “Talking Tom & Frie
body:
“Talking Tom & Friends: World” has launched an in-game crossover with the iconic world of The Smurfs.

	In a partnership between “Talking Tom & Friends” owner Outfit7 (an Ekipa2 subsidiary) and Smurfs IP holder Peyo Company, the children’s mobile sandbox game “Talking Tom & Friends: World” has launched a dedicated in-game experience inspired by the classic ’80s “Smurfs” cartoon’s iconic characters, locations, and values. 


	Per the companies, “Kids can explore a Smurfs-themed scene, meet familiar faces including Papa Smurf and Smurfette, unlock themed outfits and accessories, and discover activities inspired by the Smurfs’ world.”
	

	The Smurfs collaboration marks the most recent in a growing list of outside partnerships for the “Talking Tom & Friends” franchise, which has already launched crossover projects with Barbie and “Miraculous: Tales of Ladybug and Cat Noir.”



	

	



	“Many of us grew up with the Smurfs, which is part of what makes this collaboration so special,” Outfit7 head of brand partnerships Tadeja Irmančnik said. “The Smurfs are one of those rare brands that have successfully connected with multiple generations without losing what made them special in the first place. That’s a big reason why we were excited about this partnership! Through ‘Talking Tom Friends: World,’ we’re able to bring those characters into a new type of experience and give kids another way to discover and interact with the world of the Smurfs.”

	“We are excited to bring our beloved little Smurfs into ‘Talking Tom & Friends: World’ through this new partnership with the talented team at Outfit7,” Peyo Company licensing chief Fabienne Gilles added. “I’m sure kids and parents alike will love discovering this fun new collaboration and playing together with the Smurfs, Talking Tom, and his friends.”

schema.headline: ‘Talking Tom & Friends: World’ Kids’ Mobile Game Launches The Smurfs Crossover (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Becoming Tate McRae: The Pop Sensation on Navigating Fame, Treating Work Like ‘a Fantasy’ and Getting Taylor Swift’s ‘Amazing’ Sourdough Bread
description: In early June, Tate McRae celebrated her recent move to New York by catching Knicks fever. It was less than a year since she relocated from Los Ange
body:
In early June, Tate McRae celebrated her recent move to New York by catching Knicks fever. It was less than a year since she relocated from Los Angeles, where she kick-started her career as music’s next Main Pop Girl, yet she could feel the electricity coursing through her new city over a potential championship win. So she did what any young celebrity would do: She put on a Knicks T-shirt and headed up to Madison Square Garden to watch Game 4 from a suite with her close friend Hailey Bieber. “I really was the one who jumped on the bandwagon. I was like, ‘I love New York!’” says McRae with a laugh. 
	

	It’s now a few weeks later — the late afternoon of the Knicks’ victory parade — and she’s seated in a conference room of a photo studio overlooking the Flatiron District. On the streets below, vendors are hawking bootleg merchandise as stragglers from the festivities color the sidewalks with blue-and-orange jerseys and hats.



	

									David Roemer for Variety
	



	McRae, meanwhile, is just trying to blend in. Near the end of the shoot, she glides from room to room, swarmed by her team. Few heads turn despite her tall, unmistakable frame shuffling across the floor. As much as she has been seen these days — which has been a lot, to the tune of more than a million Tater Tots (her fandom name) at her latest tour — she’s still unsure how to deal with the glare of thousands of iPhones. She’s figuring herself out, like any 23-year-old would, by clinging to her journal.

	“You’ve gotta learn yourself. You have to write down, ‘What are my favorite songs? What are my favorite colors? What are my favorite references? What are my favorite movies?’” she says. “That, I think, shapes your identity and hopefully comes across through you as the vessel.”
	

	It’s been about seven months since she concluded her “Miss Possessive” tour, an 88-date worldwide trek that grossed more than $100 million, and she’s finally coming back down to earth. The experience was unparalleled for anyone her age, bringing the kind of attention that sends our best and brightest stars into spectacular spirals. (Think Britney Spears, with whom she’s endlessly compared.) For McRae, the concerts were so overwhelming that she can’t even recall the finale at Los Angeles’ Kia Forum in November. When asked about her electric piano not cooperating as she stood behind the keyboard that night, she draws a blank: “I have early signs of dementia, I think, because I can’t remember anything that’s ever happened to me.” 

	To the world, McRae is a strong, fearless entertainer, a triple threat who can pen songs that recall the fizzy pop of the early aughts and bring them to life as a ferocious singer and dancer. But in her new home, she’s relishing the cloak of anonymity that only New York can offer. She set up shop in NoHo, frequenting her local coffee shop and going for hot Pilates. She’s read some books — recommending Sidney Sheldon’s 1982 thriller “Master of the Game” — and learned how to cook three things: ground turkey, eggs and sweet potatoes, the latter of which she makes in an air fryer. On some days, she’ll walk through Washington Square Park or talk with random strangers; on others, she’ll log on to Zoom for meetings with her team. 

	Life is, for now, normal, whatever that means. But that’s about as normal as it can get for a pop star of McRae’s standing. Over the past few years, the Canadian native has risen from a YouTube upstart to what some are christening Gen-Z’s answer to Spears. Her breakthrough sophomore album, 2023’s “Think Later,” was a purposeful shift from introspective balladry to Y2K-era pop, spawning the Nelly Furtado-indebted single “Greedy,” which climbed to No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100. A little over a year later, McRae hit full throttle with “So Close to What,” which bowed atop the albums chart in February 2025. Not long after, she scored her first Grammy nomination with the slick “Just Keep Watching” off the “F1: The Movie” soundtrack. 
	

	Amid it all, McRae’s stock continued to rise in celebrity circles. Following the Grammys, where she came up empty-handed, she put the loss behind her at Charli xcx’s after-party. In May, she made her Met Gala debut in custom Ludovic de Saint Sernin and held hands with Blackpink’s Rosé as they stepped into GQ’s post-gala fete. After the Knicks’ historic Game 4 win, McRae and Bieber headed down to the club Zero Bond to hobnob with Sombr, the Haim sisters and Taylor Swift, who had previously sent her a homemade loaf of sourdough bread. 



	

									David Roemer for Variety
	



	“The basket smelled amazing,” McRae recalls, leaning forward as though she’s letting me in on a secret. “I don’t know what perfume she wears, but I was like, ‘She must smell incredible.’” 

	In July, Swift invited McRae to attend the wedding of the century at Madison Square Garden, and a few weeks later, McRae was back in Los Angeles to deliver the match ball at the opening of a FIFA World Cup game. 

	“I think she just stands out so distinctly,” says Bieber, who attended husband Justin Bieber’s Skylrk World Cup party with McRae following Spain’s title win on July 19. “You can’t help but want to listen and watch her. She works her ass off. She’s making a clear mark.” It only helps, adds Bieber in an email, that McRae is gracious with those she chooses to keep company with: “Tate is as sweet as they come. I may be biased when I say I love a Canadian” — like her husband — “but I really do. She is salt of the earth, grounded and always fun to be around.” 

	At Blonde Studios in New York City, McRae appears to be enjoying the leisurely pace of a photo shoot. She’s tried on several looks and ends the day in jeans and a denim-meets-tiger-print spaghetti-strap top. She loves the jeans so much, in fact, that she asks her team if she can keep them. You wouldn’t know it from her bubbly disposition, but her songs tend to be the tell: McRae can’t help facing her darkest thoughts in her music. It’s evident on songs like “Nostalgia,” where she sings of having “a lot to lose, so I might as well lose it anyway,” or on “Horseshoe,” a cinematic tune in which she asks, “Where should my sadness go?” 

	McRae speaks as though a giggle is always on the verge of escaping her lips. But she’s clearly overcome by her inner monologue. As she discusses the swings of her career, she’s candid about the pressures of fame and its often crushing weight. She looks back on the emotional comedown from the “Miss Possessive” tour, for instance, and muses about just how deeply it embedded itself under her skin. 
	

	“I remember reading Sylvia Plath being like, ‘I am her,’” she says as she lets out a small laugh. “My thoughts felt so dark at the time, and I felt so lonely. I really needed to come back into my body and regulate my nervous system. I was so shot after the tour. I couldn’t really sleep at night. I’d seen so much of myself that I was like, ‘I want to go into a black room and not look in a mirror for six months.’ And I think I really had to check myself and be like, ‘You’re not the worst person in the world. You’re not the ugliest person in the world. You haven’t done everything wrong. And, you know, you’re just doing what you love.’”



	

									David Roemer for Variety
	



	McRae has turned to the stage to establish some semblance of stability. Performing, she says, is where she feels most at home. Much like Beyoncé’s Sasha Fierce, she inhabits a character onstage named Tatiana, who allows her to tap into the raw energy that powers her shows. She’s at her peak when she’s dancing and singing; remove the dancing, and she’s slightly less confident. Put her onstage to accept an award and give a speech, and her anxiety kicks into high gear.

	“Sometimes in smaller rooms, you feel more nervous than [in front of] 20,000 people, and you start to target why you feel nervous and why you don’t try to overcome that,” she says. Dancing is her sweet spot, and she’s gone viral time and again for her exacting moves. Her performance from last year’s MTV Video Music Awards, a showstopping medley of the zippy “Sports Car” and “Revolving Door,” was just nominated for a 2026 Emmy. “I think it’s muscle memory. When I was a kid feeling awkward in my skin or feeling uncomfortable, dancing was my way of feeling cool and feeling like I excelled at something. And I think I feel that way when I perform, like I’m in my element.”


	McRae has been nurturing her passion for performance since she was 6, studying ballet in her native Calgary before expanding her love of the arts to music. In 2017, she began posting original songs on YouTube via her “Create With Tate” series that, two years later, led to her signing with RCA. Her first album, 2022’s “I Used to Think I Could Fly,” might as well have been from an entirely different artist, one who wallowed in her feelings on ballads with grim titles like “Hate Myself” and “Feel Like Shit.”

	It was with “Think Later” and, subsequently, “So Close to What” that she found her footing, quite literally, by marrying her love of choreography with her propensity for singing and songwriting. (“Sad girl bit got a little boring,” she admits on “Think Later” opener “Cut My Hair.”) It was all in service of the spectacle — McRae meticulously delivers bespoke performances for almost all her gigs, whether as musical guest on “Saturday Night Live,” twice, or at events like the iHeartRadio Music Festival and the Billboard Music Awards.
	



	

									David Roemer for Variety
	



	She manages all this, she says, by treating work like play: “Our biggest thing is romanticizing and making everything so fun. It’s like, let’s go rent a pink Jeep and romanticize the shit out of this experience. That keeps life very light and exciting and a bit like a fantasy, which is the only way to approach this because it can come with a lot of pressure.”

	McRae tries to stay in control as much as she can. Her songs have elicited speculation online about their subjects, as though they are the Rosetta stone of Tate McRae. “So Close to What” is assumed to be about her then-boyfriend, rapper the Kid Laroi, who is featured on one of its songs. After a year and a half of dating, they split last summer, and in September, McRae released the scathing kiss-off “Tit for Tat,” which was largely believed to be about the betrayal she felt from the breakup. (“My dad hates you, my dog hates you, my brother hates you and I do too / I asked all of California, they all happy that you moved,” she sings on “Anything but Love” from the deluxe edition of “So Close to What.” The songs sent some corners of the internet into overdrive.)

	For her own sanity, McRae prefers to float above the noise, staying out of the discourse and letting the work speak for itself. “If you think about the reception while you’re creating, you’re destroying the process. Thinking about reception and people interpreting is so terrifying to me,” she says.

	McRae has famously disavowed X, instead curating her online presence with carefully deployed posts on Instagram and TikTok: “I’m always shocked by how much people speculate and talk about things. It’s really scary. So I try not to read it, and let it drift off into the wind.”

	That also means walking a tightrope of keeping her relationships out of the public eye. Just a day before the photo shoot, celebrity gossip account DeuxMoi published a post speculating on the status of her romance with New Jersey Devils center Jack Hughes, with whom she was linked earlier this year. It’s not a stretch, given her fierce hockey fandom: On the cover of “Think Later,” she wears hockey pads — a very Canadian move — and she was a celebrity co-captain with Justin Bieber and Michael Bublé at the 2024 NHL All-Star Game.
	

	“I try to keep my relationships as sacred and private as possible,” she says. She’s careful about how much she reveals, taking a moment to collect her thoughts before continuing. “I love the people in my life. They love me. You just try to keep that circle as positive and supportive as possible. And the outside noise, I can’t do anything about that. Focusing my energy on something that I can’t control, it just puts me in a bad mood.”



	

									David Roemer for Variety
	



	Things she can’t control? Last year, she duetted with Morgan Wallen on the song “What I Want,” which debuted at No. 1 on the Hot 100 but enabled the internet to brand her as a MAGA supporter by association with the country singer. Her relationship with Hughes only strengthened that narrative after his team laughed at a distasteful joke made by President Trump during a congratulatory call following their Olympic win earlier this year.

	I ask her why it’s important for her not to tread into that sort of conversation. “I like to say my piece through organizations I support and the environment that I have on tour,” she says. Last year, for instance, she posted a TikTok advertising a “Little Miss Possessive” hoodie, with a portion of proceeds going to The Trevor Project, a nonprofit focusing on suicide prevention for LGBTQ+ youth, and Global Fund for Women. “I think it’s pretty obvious what kind of person I am and the things I support. And I hope that my fans can see that through the things that I’m putting my energy towards.”


	As she navigates the choppy waters of superstardom, McRae has been finding comfort in her family. At the photo shoot, her mother, Tanja Rosner, sits in the adjacent room with McRae’s manager as the crew packs up. Usually her mom is back in Canada, and they talk to each other, McRae says, “around seven times a day.” “I’m living with my mom on FaceTime,” she adds, often starting her day by having a virtual coffee with her. Her only sibling, Tucker, who just graduated from Dartmouth, is about to come live with her in New York. She goes home a few times a year, mainly for her birthday and Christmas, to see her parents, grandfather and friends.

	She’s also begun work on her fourth album, which is in the see-what-sticks phase. She had her first session for the project in February with hit songwriters Amy Allen and Emile Haynie, whose collective credits include everyone from Sabrina Carpenter and Lana Del Rey to Olivia Rodrigo and Harry Styles. As with her past records, McRae is mood-boarding much of the project but still doesn’t know how it will take shape. All she really says about it is that she flips through a Dolly Parton coffee-table book filled with her lyrics for inspiration and has some of the country legend’s songs on a playlist she calls “Bubbly Bubbly Brain Refresh.” She avoids listening to straightforward pop music while writing and recording; it leaves her uninspired.

	As the sun begins to set on New York City, McRae says she’s looking toward the two major festival appearances looming on the calendar. She’s headlining Montreal’s Osheaga Festival and Chicago’s Lollapalooza, taking place on the same weekend in early August, and rehearsals are starting in a few weeks. A lot is riding on Osheaga, she says, since it’s her first time performing at a festival in Canada. She knows it needs to be above her standard, which is already impossibly high.
	

	“There’s always thought about how you want your legacy to go down,” she says. “For me, the way to do that is try to beat your last performance, try to beat your last song, try to grow, evolve, pick it apart, rip it apart, figure out what didn’t work, what I didn’t like about that performance, what I could have done better, why I was nervous, figure out how to not be nervous. I think the more you can master yourself and your performances, the better you get.”

title: The CW Picks Up Additional Seasons of ‘Scrabble,’ ‘Trivial Pursuit,’ ‘Police 24/7’
description: The CW is renewing three of its unscripted series The one-hour gamers “Scrabble” and “Trivial Pursuit” have been given a Season 3 in advance of this
body:
The CW is renewing three of its unscripted series The one-hour gamers “Scrabble” and “Trivial Pursuit” have been given a Season 3 in advance of this fall’s Season 2 premieres, while the netlet has also greenlighted a Season 4 of its law enforcement follow-along show “Police 24/7.”

	“Scrabble” and “Trivial Pursuit” return to The CW on Thursday, Oct. 1 with their Season 2 premieres; the shows’ Season 3 episodes will come at a later date.
	

	Seperately, “Scrabble,” “Trivial Pursuit” and “Police 24/7” have also been sold into daytime syndication; according to The CW, the shows’ syndie runs have now been cleared in more than 85% of U.S. TV markets. Wallach Media Ventures is distributing.


	According to The CW, the three shows were among the network’s top five most-watched entertainment programs during the 2025-2026 season. Per The CW, the three shows “have collectively reached more than 31.4 million viewers on The CW since debuting and generated more than 1.2 million viewing hours across The CW’s digital platforms.”

	Craig Ferguson hosts “Scrabble,” which “brings the iconic Hasbro word game to life as contestants put their vocabulary, strategy and quick thinking to the test for the chance to win life-changing cash prizes” Hasbro Entertainment, The CW, Mattel Television Studios and Lionsgate Alternative Television are the producers.

	LeVar Burton hosts “Trivial Pursuit,” which “transforms one of the world’s most recognizable trivia brands into a fast-paced competition where contestants put their knowledge to the test across a wide range of categories.” Hasbro Entertainment, The CW, Lionsgate Alternative Television and Talpa Studios are the producers.
	

	SallyAnn Salsano and her Mulholland Media are behind “Police 24/7,” which “provides unprecedented access to law enforcement agencies across the country, following officers on patrol as they respond to emergencies, investigate crimes and serve their communities.”

schema.headline: The CW Picks Up Additional Seasons of ‘Scrabble,’ ‘Trivial Pursuit,’ ‘Police 24/7’

title: ‘Spider-Man’ Beats ‘Avengers: Endgame’ as ‘Brand New Day’ Climbs to $360 Million, the Biggest Opening Weekend in Box Office History
description:
Is Spider-Man more powerful than all of the Avengers combined?

	There’s certainly a case to be made after “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” captured a mi
body:
Is Spider-Man more powerful than all of the Avengers combined?

	There’s certainly a case to be made after “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” captured a mind-boggling, record-setting $360 million in its domestic debut, officially ranking as the biggest debut in box office history. After landing above Sunday’s estimates of $355 million, “Brand New Day” has outpaced the prior all-time benchmark of 2019’s “Avengers: Endgame” with $357 million (not adjusted for inflation). 
	

	“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “Avengers: Endgame” are historic as the only two movies in history to cross $300 million in a single weekend. To put those ticket sales in perspective, those behemoths earned around $100 million more to start than the third-and fourth-largest domestic openings, which belong to 2021’s “Spider-Man: No Way Home” with $260 million and 2018’s “Avengers: Infinity War” with $257 million. The top four-biggest debuts in box office history belong to Marvel Studios.


	“Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” Sony and Marvel’s fourth comic-book adventure starring Tom Holland as Peter Parker, launched to a truly heroic $932 million globally, a benchmark that few films achieve by the end of their box office runs, much less after three days on the big screen. It’s the second-biggest worldwide debut, trailing only “Avengers: Endgame” with $1.2 billion. 

	“Wow! 360 million thank-yous to all the filmmakers, actors, producers, and to my colleagues at Sony, who created such a fantastic film and an exceptional marketing and distribution campaign,” says Tom Rothman, chairman of Sony Pictures. “Records are made to be broken, but we will take great pride in this one, for as long as we hold it.”
	

	“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” set all kinds of records in its first weekend of release, including the largest preview haul with $72 million, as well as the biggest opening day with $169.8 million. With euphoric word-of-mouth (and without much competition), this Spidey adventure is poised to dominate on the big screen throughout the rest of summer. It should easily surpass $2 billion globally, a milestone that only seven movies in history have ever achieved.

	Destin Daniel Cretton (“Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings”) directed “Brand New Day,” which picks up after the events of “No Way Home” — which ended with the entire world forgetting about Peter Parker. He’s still fighting crime, though, as a mysterious entity threatens New York City. Busting baddies has been all the more difficult for Spider-Man, not just because he’s sorely missing his girlfriend MJ (Zendaya) and best friend Ned (Jacob Batalon), neither of whom remember he exists, but also because he’s struggling with his mutating powers. 

	Holland’s run as Spider-Man has been especially impressive as the rare property to keep growing at the box office. His first solo outing 2017’s “Homecoming,” opened to $117 million domestically and climbed to $880 million worldwide. The 2019 sequel “Far From Home” launched to $92 million domestically and ended with a mighty $1.13 billion worldwide. Then the third adventure “No Way Home” powered to $260 million domestically and ended its run with a colossal with $1.9 billion worldwide. Holland has teased that succession plans are already in the works for Peter Parker, but after this historic weekend, it’s safe to say he’s not retiring just yet.

schema.headline: ‘Spider-Man’ Beats ‘Avengers: Endgame’ as ‘Brand New Day’ Climbs to $360 Million, the Biggest Opening Weekend in Box Office History

title: ‘Sex Lives of College Girls’ Star Gavin Leatherwood Joins Nina Dobrev in Rom-Com ‘It Happened One Summer,’ Adapted From BookTok Hit
description: “Chilling Adventures of Sabrina” breakout and “Sex Lives of College Girls” star Gavin Leatherwood has joined the cast of romantic comedy “It Happene
body:
“Chilling Adventures of Sabrina” breakout and “Sex Lives of College Girls” star Gavin Leatherwood has joined the cast of romantic comedy “It Happened One Summer,” the adaptation of Tessa Bailey’s New York Tiles bestseller and viral BookTok hit. 

	Production on the film is now underway in New York, with Leatherwood joining an ensemble that already includes Nina Dobrev (“The Out-Laws,” “The Bricklayer”), Tyler Hoechlin (“Superman & Lois”) and Virginia Gardner (“Fall,” “Halloween”). Peter Hutchings (“The Hating Game”) directs.
	

	Written by “The Hating Game” scribe Christina Mengert and Joseph Muszynski, “It Happened One Summer” is being produced by BCDF Pictures (“To Leslie,” “Which Brings Me to You”), with Frolic Media executive producing alongside Dobrev, Hoechlin, Gardner and Bailey. Embankment handles worldwide sales and has extensively pre-sold the title.


	The film follows Piper Bellinger, a glamorous L.A. It Girl whose glittering world comes crashing down after a viral mishap gets her canceled overnight. Cut off from her wealthy family’s safety net, she is exiled to a rugged fishing town with one ultimatum: fix up her late father’s dive bar – or lose everything. There, she butts heads with Brendan, a gruff sea captain who has zero patience for influencers. As per the description, Brendan is “the last person she expected – and exactly what she needs.” But he’s not the only sexy sea dog around, with Leatherwood set to play Fox Thornton, “a charismatic ladies’ man whose easy charm masks a deeper loyalty and vulnerability.”

	“It wasn’t easy to find someone with the charm and swagger of Fox Thornton, but we did it! So thrilled to have Gavin on board,” said Bailey.
	

	“Gavin was the missing piece — he walked in and the whole cast lifted,” added Hutchings. “Nina and Virginia are brilliant together as the Bellinger sisters, and with Tyler and Gavin alongside them, we’ve got something really special.”

	“It Happened One Summer” has been translated into 25 languages, with two million copies sold in the U.S. alone. It is the first installment in the Bellinger Sisters series, described as one of the best-selling contemporary romance series of the past decade.

	“Tessa wrote something that makes people laugh, swoon and stay up way too late reading — we want the film to do exactly the same thing,” said producer Claude Dal Farra. “Audiences are going to have a great time with this one.” 

	Leatherwood, who most recently starred in Netflix’s “It’s What’s Inside,” which premiered at Sundance and was acquired by the streamer for $17 million, is repped by Verve and Entertainment 360.

schema.headline: ‘Sex Lives of College Girls’ Star Gavin Leatherwood Joins Nina Dobrev in Rom-Com ‘It Happened One Summer,’ Adapted From BookTok Hit

title: Low Light Films Boards Locarno Competition Thriller ‘O Jacaré,’ Basil Da Cunha Celebration of Lisbon’s Vibrant Reboleira District (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Deep in the mazework neighborhood of Reboleira, Lisbon, someone is hiding €180,000 ($200,000), and Portuguese-Swiss writer-director Basil Da Cunha a
body:
Deep in the mazework neighborhood of Reboleira, Lisbon, someone is hiding €180,000 ($200,000), and Portuguese-Swiss writer-director Basil Da Cunha allows the characters of “O Jacaré” to use any and all means to find it in his new feature film competing at Locarno. 

	Produced by Thera Production (Switzerland) and co-produced by Continue Walking (Portugal) and RTS Radio Télévision Suisse, “O Jacaré” wastes no time dropping its audience in the middle of a vibrant, interwoven community, using Cape Verdean music and an ensemble cast of locals to set the tension of the plot.
	

	The film, which will compete in Locarno’s main International Competition, has been boarded by Barcelona-based Low Light Films ahead of its world premiere. 


	“From the moment we saw ‘O Jacaré,’ we knew it was a film we wanted to champion,” said Jainer Morales Mena, Low Light Films founder. “We’re incredibly proud to represent it internationally and to help bring it to audiences around the world.”

	“O Jacaré” is Da Cunha’s final film set in Reboleira, as the district faces pending demolition, and he uses the feature to celebrate an era of life there. Much of the film is sun-soaked and colorful and filled with the rhythm and chaos of life in a cloistered, liminal community. Although structured around the search for the missing money, “O Jacaré” is interested in solving a mystery but all the more in observing the stylings of Reboleira itself, and it’s in this meditation on time and place that the film finds its heart.



	

					Basil Da Cunha directs ‘O Jacaré.’
									Courtesy of Low Light Films
	



	Ahead of the film’s premiere, Variety spoke with Da Cunha about returning to Locarno, as well as his bond to Reboleira. 
	

	How has your relationship with Reboleira evolved over the many years filming there, and how did that shape “O Jacaré?”

	For more than 20 years, cinema has grown alongside the people of Reboleira. It gradually stopped being something I brought into the neighborhood and became part of the neighborhood itself. Entire families have appeared in my films across generations as actors, extras, crew members or simply witnesses. We raised children together, buried friends, celebrated weddings and watched streets disappear. “O Jacaré” comes from that shared history. It isn’t just a film about Reboleira; it’s a film made from within it. As the neighborhood slowly disappears through demolition, I felt an urgency to preserve its gestures, voices, humor, music and memories before they vanished. In many ways, the film is both a celebration and an act of remembrance.

	What drew you to telling this story through such a large ensemble of characters rather than following a single protagonist?

	I’ve never experienced Reboleira as a place of individual heroes. It’s a collective world where everyone’s story constantly overlaps with everyone else’s. I wanted the film to move like the neighborhood itself: unpredictable, noisy, full of encounters and digressions. Every character carries a different generation, a different dream, a different wound. But the ensemble structure also came from another desire: “O Jacaré” is the last dance of the body of work I’ve built in Reboleira over the past 15 years. I felt an urgency to bring everyone together before this world disappeared. Some of the streets no longer exist, children have become adults, and many people have moved away. I wanted to reunite, in a single film, all the generations of people I’ve worked with throughout that journey. The film becomes both a story and a reunion: a collective portrait of a community, but also of the cinematic family we’ve built together over the years.

	Music plays a massive role in the spirit of the film. Can you talk about your process for approaching the music of the story?

	Music isn’t something I add to the film afterwards; it’s part of the life I’m filming. Most of the songs come from Cape Verdean musicians who shaped the cultural identity of the community long before I arrived. They carry memory, exile, celebration and melancholy all at once. I wanted every piece of music to feel as if it naturally belonged to the space, whether it’s heard from a passing car, a bar, a party or inside someone’s home. Rather than illustrating emotion, the music creates the emotional landscape the characters already inhabit. I also wanted the film itself to move like the music. The rhythm of the editing, the energy of the scenes and even the humor are deeply influenced by Cape Verdean funk from the 1970s. For the first time, I wanted to fully embrace the pleasure of popular genre cinema, not as an ironic reference, but as a genuine way of telling the stories of people who are rarely allowed to become larger-than-life cinematic figures. Music became the heartbeat that holds all of that together.
	

	What does it mean for “O Jacaré” to premiere in Locarno’s International Competition, especially given your long history with the festival?

	Locarno has accompanied almost my entire journey as a filmmaker. My first short film screened there in 2009, and many important moments of my career have passed through the festival since then. “O Jacaré” is now the third feature film I’ve premiered in Locarno, which makes this selection especially meaningful. It’s a recognition not only of my work, but of everyone in Reboleira who trusted cinema enough to make it part of their lives. In many ways, it feels like bringing the neighborhood onto one of the world’s biggest stages.

schema.headline: Low Light Films Boards Locarno Competition Thriller ‘O Jacaré,’ Basil Da Cunha Celebration of Lisbon’s Vibrant Reboleira District (EXCLUSIVE)

            A survivor of the Oct. 7 music festival attack in Israel was found dead at his girlfriend's grave ... nearly three years after she was murdered by Hamas.
      
    
            Bar Asraf reportedly died by suicide Saturday at a cemetery in the West Bank settlement of Elkana, according to Israeli news site JFeed. His girlfriend, Liron Barda, was among the hundreds killed during the October 2023 Nova music festival massacre.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Barda was working as a bartender at the festival when Hamas terrorists stormed the event ... and she stayed behind to help wounded festivalgoers before she was killed.
      

            Her father later said he had urged her to leave, but she told him people were hurt and she intended to stay.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Asraf and Barda both died young ... he was 30, and she was 26.
      
    
            He reportedly remained close with Barda's family after her death, frequently visiting her parents and continuing to honor her memory.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Asraf's death comes as survivors and victims' families continue dealing with the lasting trauma of the Oct. 7 massacre, which left nearly 400 dead and dozens more taken hostage.

Cyclosporiasis Outbreak
                          2 People Dead in Michigan

                              August 3, 2026
                            9:33 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            2 people have died in the cyclosporiasis outbreak, according to the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services.
      
    
            The MDHHS updated their case numbers Monday, listing that there have been 2 deaths since the infectious disease spread through the state.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The victims weren't identified, but the announcement noted that their medical records showed "significant underlying health conditions that may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration."
      

            MDHHS says they won't be providing any other information on these cases.
      
    
            According to the department, cyclosporiasis itself is "generally not a life-threatening illness." They note that dying from it is "uncommon" in the U.S.
      
    
            Based on their numbers, over 11K people in Michigan have reported cases of cyclosporiasis ... and 193 of them indicated they'd been hospitalized.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The FDA's probe of the outbreak had pointed the finger towards Taco Bell's lettuce supplier, Taylor Farms, but they've since said those tests resulted in a false positive.

title: Ariana Grande Pulls Out of London Stage Revival with Jonathan Bailey Amid Public Scrutiny
description:
Ariana Grande
                          Drops Out of Show with Jonathan Bailey ...
body:
Ariana Grande
                          Drops Out of Show with Jonathan Bailey ...
                          Amid Public Criticism
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              
                August 2, 2026
                
                            4:30 PM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 3, 2026
                                7:30 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Ariana Grande isn't just stepping away from the spotlight following her "Eternal Sunshine Tour," she's hitting pause on her acting career and chance to reunite with former co-star Jonathan Bailey.
      
    
            The pop superstar has officially withdrawn from the upcoming London revival of Stephen Sondheim's "Sunday in the Park With George," where she had been set to work again with her 'Wicked' co-star at the Barbican in 2027.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Grande's rep said in a statement to PEOPLE the decision is part of a broader plan to take a break from public-facing work once she wraps up her massively successful "Eternal Sunshine Tour" and intends to "take a step back from visibility" after the tour concludes
      

            According to the rep, Grande wants to finish the run "on a high note, both healthily and happily," before taking what her team describes as a "much-deserved break."
      
    
            The statement also points to the downside of fame, saying public appearances have subjected Grande to "endless, ongoing public scrutiny." Her rep added that Ariana has loved every minute of performing for fans during the tour and is grateful for the experience, but now feels it's time to prioritize herself.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            That means "Sunday in the Park With George" is officially off her calendar. The show's official account confirmed the acclaimed musical will still move forward as planned despite Grande's exit. Her role will be recast before the show opens at London's Barbican.
      
    
            The revival had generated major buzz thanks to the planned reunion of Grande and Bailey following their performances in 'Wicked,' making her departure a significant shake-up for theater fans.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As for Ariana, it sounds like the next chapter won't involve red carpets, premieres or Broadway stages ... at least not for a while. After years of nonstop music, movies and public attention, she's choosing to step out of the spotlight and recharge.
